initial_presentation: A 14-year-old boy with no prior health issues presented with left periorbital swelling and redness persisting for 1 year, along with muscle weakness and joint pain for 4 months. Physical examination revealed purple discoloration and swelling around the left eye, Gottron's papules over the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints on both hands, and muscle weakness graded at 3/5 in the proximal muscles and 4/5 in the distal muscles.

A 36-year-old female patient presented with multiple lesions that first appeared during childhood and have progressively increased in number and size over time. The patient reported that the lesions were painful with minimal trauma. Physical examination revealed blue-purple papules and nodules ranging from a few millimeters to nearly 2 cm in size, grouped in plaques averaging 10 cm on the epigastric and right inguinocrural regions. On the right hemithorax, the lesions exhibited a zosteriform pattern, while on the upper limbs, the lesions were sparse. The patient reported no similar cases in her family.
A 56-year-old woman experienced chest tightness, chronic cough, and sputum production for three years, which did not improve with treatment at local hospitals. She was referred to our hospital.
A 29-year-old male presented with abnormal findings on a urine dipstick test, showing the presence of blood and protein.

The patient is a 35-year-old male with a history of jaundice since birth, with total bilirubin (TB) levels ranging from 70–80 µmol/L. In adulthood, his TB levels increased to approximately 300 µmol/L. At the age of 31, he experienced right upper abdominal pain and severe jaundice, with TB levels rising above 500 µmol/L. He was found to have gallbladder stones and cholecystitis. Treatment with antibiotics and oral phenobarbital alleviated his pain and reduced TB to 300 µmol/L. Subsequently, he had recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, fever, and severe jaundice. In November 2019, he became lethargic and unresponsive following a fever, and later developed limb convulsions and urinary incontinence.
A 10-year-old girl presented with a 2-week history of continuous headache, which was worsened by accompanying nausea.

A 14-year-old female presented with severe lower abdominal and back pain persisting for the past 3 months. The pain, colicky in nature and radiating to the back, was often accompanied by nausea and vomiting, beginning with the onset of her menstrual cycle and lasting for 5 to 7 days. She also experienced urinary retention 24 hours before admission. She had her first menstrual period at age 10 and had regular cycles every 28 days with scanty flow. Her pregnancy and birth were unremarkable, and there was no family history of congenital anomalies. She had no other health issues since birth, was not sexually active, and was not using contraceptives. A few months prior, she developed severe dysmenorrhea, leading her caretakers to consult a general practitioner, who provided symptomatic treatment with an antispasmodic agent and analgesic, resulting in brief symptom relief. She was then referred to a tertiary care center for further management. On general examination, she had mild anemia, and abdominal examination revealed a tense urinary bladder. Per vaginal examination showed a bulged hymen with obstructed hemivagina. She was afebrile with normal vital signs.

A 3.5-year-old girl was referred to a tertiary care hospital in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia for evaluation of congenital contractures on August 6, 2011. The patient's mother reported a full-term normal pregnancy with normal fetal movements. Delivery was via cesarean section due to prolonged labor. The patient was born with contractures affecting her fingers, knees, and feet. These contractures improved over time with periodic physiotherapy, particularly in her thumbs and 4th and 5th fingers, which were often flexed into the palm. The patient is reported to be cognitively intelligent, with speech and language development in the 99th percentile. She was able to crawl and stand on her knees at an early age. The patient is not on any medications, has no known allergies, and has never been hospitalized or had surgery. She is followed regularly by orthopedics for consideration of soft tissue release, particularly for current talipes more pronounced on the left side. She also has pterygium webbing of the knee joints, limiting extension. The family pedigree revealed that the parents are double first-degree cousins, and they have two girls and one boy who are healthy with no similar family history reported. Upon arrival at the hospital, physical examination showed the following: temperature 37.1°C, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, pulse rate 96 beats/min, blood pressure 110/60 mmHg, and blood oxygen saturation 96%. Weight was 9.5 kg, head circumference was 45 cm, and cranial nerve examination was unremarkable. Distinct dysmorphic facial features were noted, including a triangular face with micrognathia, prominent forehead, narrow palpebral fissures, deep-set eyes, and low-set ears. There was no tongue fasciculation. Neuromuscular assessment showed isometric strength around the shoulders and elbows, with relatively preserved strength in finger flexion. The hands showed mild deformity of the 4th and 5th fingers, with creases present and no obvious hypothenar muscle eminence. In the lower extremities, there was clear thinning of the leg muscles compared to the thighs, associated with pterygium behind both knees limiting extension. Achilles tendon shortening was more noticeable on the left side with inversion, and limited ankle dorsiflexion was observed on the right side with distal weakness. Reflexes were difficult to elicit, but responses were +1 around the knees and biceps level. Examination of the back showed subtle scoliosis, and when pulled to a sitting position, the head lagged and the patient was unable to hold her head up for long periods, though she was not very cooperative according to her parents.

A 61-year-old female experienced a cardiac arrest at home. Her husband performed CPR until the emergency physician arrived. Upon arrival, ventricular fibrillation was addressed with defibrillation. Subsequent asystole was converted to ventricular tachycardia with norepinephrine. The addition of amiodarone resulted in a stable sinus rhythm. Upon arrival at the clinic, mask ventilation was replaced with endotracheal intubation. Mild therapeutic hypothermia was initiated and maintained for 24 hours. The patient was extubated after 48 hours.
A 75-year-old Caucasian male with a prolonged history of retinal changes was evaluated in the clinic. He initially presented in 1985 with pigmentary changes at the macula observed by his optician.
